subtype: Approach: talking to people who do the work [Action]
passage: Dear Vishal Bhaiya, thank you for spending Sunday's call telling your little cousin what a chartered accountant actually does all day. I've now asked three people: you, the architect whose office is near the bus stand, and our neighbour who is a nurse. In my notebook I wrote what each said was boring or stressful. You: matching bills line by line, and March deadlines. The architect: site visits in the heat, and clients who change their minds after the drawing is done. The nurse: standing for hours and night shifts, but she said one thank-you from a patient makes up for a lot. Reading the notes, I noticed the boring parts scare me less than the changing-minds part. I'll ask more questions before choosing anything. Love, Salma

qa.q: Which people did Salma ask about their day, besides the cousin?
qa.a: The architect near the bus stand and the nurse neighbour.

qa.q: What might Salma be feeling on rereading the notes?
qa.a: Thoughtful and slightly uneasy: the boring parts scare Salma less than clients who change their minds, so Salma wants to ask more before choosing.

qa.q: What else could Salma do to test her interest, and why?
qa.a: Spend a day observing or helping at one workplace, since a short tryout shows whether a real working day suits Salma better than descriptions do.

qa.q: How might the nurse neighbour see Salma's questions?
qa.a: The nurse is asked about a real day and not just the job title, so they may value the honest interest and feel free to describe the hard parts as well.

grounding: A student asks a cousin, an architect and a nurse neighbour about a normal day and records the boring and stressful parts.
